reactions.name: Methane burns
reactions.note: Natural gas in air: once lit, its own heat keeps it going until the fuel or the oxygen runs out.

reactions.name: Carbon monoxide burns
reactions.note: The blue flame over glowing charcoal: carbon monoxide meeting air and burning on.

reactions.name: Hydrogen burns
reactions.note: Rocket fuel: the reverse of electrolysis, giving the energy back.

reactions.name: Charcoal burns
reactions.note: Carbon burning completely, where there's air enough.

reactions.name: Charcoal smoulders
reactions.note: Hot carbon short of air makes carbon monoxide: what a furnace needs.

reactions.name: CO₂ meets hot carbon
reactions.note: Above about 1000 K, CO₂ passing over glowing carbon turns into carbon monoxide (the Boudouard reaction).

reactions.name: Iron is smelted
reactions.note: Carbon monoxide pulls the oxygen out of iron ore. Slow below red heat.

reactions.name: Malachite breaks down
reactions.note: Green ore turns black in a fire, giving off CO₂ and steam.

reactions.name: Copper is smelted
reactions.note: The first metal people won from rock: easier than iron, in a hot, smoky fire.

reactions.name: Water is split
reactions.note: Electric current through water: hydrogen and oxygen at two to one. Fuel and air from ice.

reactions.name: Iron rusts
reactions.note: Slow, and only with liquid water about: iron going back to ore.

reactions.name: Limestone is burned
reactions.note: A kiln above about 1100 K drives CO₂ out of limestone, leaving quicklime.

reactions.name: Photosynthesis
reactions.note: Light builds sugar from CO₂ and water and lets oxygen go: how life makes the air.

reactions.name: Copper ore is roasted
reactions.note: Brassy ore heated in air burns off its sulfur as choking fumes, leaving copper and iron oxides.

reactions.name: Tin is smelted
reactions.note: Tin ore gives up its oxygen to carbon monoxide at a bright red heat.

reactions.name: Lead ore is roasted
reactions.note: Galena burned in air: lead oxide and sulfur dioxide.

reactions.name: Lead is smelted
reactions.note: Lead comes easily: a hot fire is enough.

reactions.name: Magnetite is smelted
reactions.note: Black iron ore, smelted like red.

reactions.name: Pyrite is roasted
reactions.note: Fool's gold burns to iron oxide and sulfur dioxide.

reactions.name: Sulfur burns
reactions.note: A blue flame and choking smoke.

reactions.name: Clay is fired
reactions.note: Above about 800 K clay gives up the water locked in it and turns to pottery for good.

reactions.name: Bronze is alloyed
reactions.note: Molten copper and molten tin, stirred together: bronze. Both must be liquid.

reactions.name: Iron soaks up carbon
reactions.note: Molten iron in contact with charcoal takes carbon in, becoming cast iron.

reactions.name: Carbon is blown out of iron
reactions.note: Air blown through molten cast iron burns most of its carbon away: steel.

reactions.name: Pewter is alloyed
reactions.note: Molten tin and a little molten lead.

reactions.name: Wood burns
reactions.note: A fire: once lit it feeds itself while there's air.

reactions.name: Wood breaks down
reactions.note: Heated, wood breaks down: charcoal stays, and carbon monoxide, methane and steam leave it. In air those gases burn as the flame; short of air they don't, and a charcoal kiln is left with the charcoal.

reactions.name: Glass is made
reactions.note: Sand and soda above about 1100 K melt together into glass.

reactions.name: Lime is slaked
reactions.note: Water on quicklime: it hisses, heats and crumbles to slaked lime.

reactions.name: Mortar sets
reactions.note: Slaked lime takes CO₂ back from the air over days and turns to stone again: lime mortar.
